extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, in-house counsel, and patent litigators (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of U.S. legal standards governing induced and indirect patent infringement, related doctrines (direct infringement, divided infringement, scienter/willful blindness), claim construction, venue, PTO guidance, and remedies. Useful for evaluating liability risk and litigation strategy in U.S. patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis for inducement (35 U.S.C. § 271(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b): 'whoever actively induces infringement of a patent shall be liable as an infringer.' The statute recognizes inducement as a form of indirect patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inducement requires affirmative conduct that causes another to infringe; the statutory phrase 'actively induces' signals a scienter/intent element. Liability serves to prevent a party who brings about infringement from escaping responsibility because another party performed the infringing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step requirement for proving inducement (direct infringement plus aiding/abetting)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show induced infringement, a plaintiff must first show that the patent was directly infringed and then that the accused party aided or abetted that infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the Supreme Court's decision rejecting 'inducement-only' liability, inducement cannot be established unless someone has committed direct infringement. Thus plaintiffs must plead and prove direct infringement (all claim steps performed) before pursuing inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scienter requirement for inducement (knowledge and affirmative intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inducement contains a knowledge/intent element: the alleged inducer must have known (or should have known) that its actions would induce actual infringement and must have had an affirmative intent to cause direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit in DSU Medical: intent requires that the alleged inducer knew or should have known its actions would induce infringement. The article notes uncertainty about how far an alleged inducer must assess patent validity or study whether induced acts infringe specific claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful blindness as a mode of proving knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Global-Tech introduced 'willful blindness' into inducement analysis, allowing imputation of requisite knowledge where the defendant deliberately avoided confirming a high probability of wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willful blindness is more than recklessness or negligence and may be proven by circumstantial evidence. The Global‑Tech standard permits liability where a defendant took deliberate actions to avoid confirming a subjective belief of a high probability of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of circumstantial evidence to satisfy scienter
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstantial evidence and inference may be used to establish the requisite knowledge and specific intent for inducement; this creates a relatively low threshold for satisfying scienter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because scienter can often be established through inference, inducement claims frequently present fact questions for juries; summary judgment for defendants may fail where material facts and reasonable inferences favor the non-moving party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement definition and strict liability (35 U.S.C. § 271(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) occurs when someone without authority makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, or imports a patented invention in the U.S. For method claims, the direct infringer must perform every claim step (literally or via equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct infringement is a strict liability tort: motive, mistake, or lack of knowledge of the patent are irrelevant. Determination requires proper claim construction and comparing claim limitations to the accused device/process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided (multiple-actor) infringement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple independent entities perform steps of a claimed method, liability for direct infringement may attach only if one entity directs or controls the other's performance or the entities form a joint enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit en banc decisions require either (1) direction/control over performance or (2) joint enterprise for finding single-entity direct infringement when steps are divided among actors. Facts showing the defendant set up the manner/timing so others must perform steps can support liability (e.g., Limelight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limelight / Supreme Court rule on inducement-only liability
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Supreme Court held that a defendant will not be liable for induced infringement under § 271(b) when no one has directly infringed the patent—i.e., inducement-only liability is rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Limelight (Supreme Court), inducement claims require an underlying finding that someone directly infringed; encouraging others to perform remaining steps is insufficient absent direct infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction importance and standards (Markman, Phillips, Teva)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is central to infringement and validity; claims are given their customary and ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art. Judges (not juries) construe claims (Markman), and Teva holds that clear-error review applies to district court factual findings in claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper claim construction precedes infringement comparison. Teva establishes that factual findings in construction are reviewed for clear error while ultimate legal issues remain de novo on appeal; Phillips guides reliance on intrinsic evidence for claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue constraints after TC Heartland
rubrics_metrics.description: For domestic corporations, 'resides' under 28 U.S.C. § 1400 means only the defendant's state of incorporation; a patent holder may sue in the state of incorporation or where the defendant commits infringing acts and has a 'regular and established place of business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This substantially narrowed venue options for patent plaintiffs compared to prior practice. Practitioners must assess corporate residence and where the defendant has a regular and established place of business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular and established place of business test (In re Cray)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit guidance (In re Cray) sets three general requirements for establishing a 'regular and established place of business' under § 1400(b): there must be (1) a physical place in the district; (2) it must be a regular and established place of business; and (3) it must be the place of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent Federal Circuit decisions (In re BigCommerce, In re HTC, In re ZTE) further clarified venue nuances (e.g., principal place of business/registered office in multi-district states; foreign companies; burden of proof on plaintiff).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines (two-step Alice/Mayo process)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's January 7, 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidelines provide a two-step process for determining whether a claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice/Mayo framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guidelines aim to provide more consistent rulings; they supersede prior guidance but note that claims previously considered eligible should remain eligible. The article emphasizes ongoing lack of clarity and shifting case law on § 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for requests for Certificates of Correction
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may request a certificate of correction under 37 C.F.R. § 1.323 to correct 'mistakes' in a patent, but 35 U.S.C. § 255 does not authorize retroactive effect after the Board's final written decision in an IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: file requests for certificate of correction before inter partes review is instituted, because after institution the Board may stay and effectively deny the patent owner's ability to obtain correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorneys' fees standard under § 285 (Octane Fitness and Highmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'exceptional' case under 35 U.S.C. § 285 is one that 'stands out' with respect to the substantive strength of a party's litigation position or the unreasonable manner in which the case was litigated; the Supreme Court lowered the burden to prove exceptionality to a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts decide exceptionality in their discretion and such decisions are reviewed for abuse of discretion rather than de novo. The Octane/Highmark decisions made fee-shifting more accessible to prevailing parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced damages under § 284 (Halo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Halo, § 284 allows courts to increase damages up to three times the amount found; the Court emphasized that 'may' should not be subject to a rigid formula and that enhanced damages are for egregious cases typified by willful misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider the particular circumstances of each case and reserve enhanced damages for culpable behavior; Halo relaxed prior rigid frameworks for awarding enhanced damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for willful infringement findings (SRI v. Cisco guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit in SRI International v. Cisco vacated a jury's willfulness finding for lack of substantial evidence, reinforcing that findings of willful infringement must be supported by substantial evidence that the conduct rose to wanton, malicious, and bad faith behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts will scrutinize factual support for enhanced damages/willfulness; mere inference without substantial evidence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent exhaustion on sale (Lexmark v. Impression Products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexmark held that when a patentee sells a product, the patentee's patent rights in that sold item are exhausted—patent law no longer controls post-sale restrictions on that article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After sale, the buyer owns the item free of patent-based control; contract remedies might remain but patent infringement suits cannot be used to enforce post-sale restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits for exported components assembled abroad (WesternGeco)
rubrics_metrics.description: WesternGeco permits patent owners to recover lost profits where the infringing party exported components from the United States for assembly abroad, so long as the relevant infringing conduct occurred in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision affects damages analyses where infringement involves exportation and foreign assembly; plaintiffs may seek U.S.-based lost profits in appropriate factual scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-adjacent procedural/other holdings (Fourth Estate copyright registration aside)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes Fourth Estate's holding in copyright law that registration is a prerequisite to filing a copyright infringement suit (included as an aside), illustrating cross-area procedural prerequisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not a patent rule, practitioners should be aware of analogous procedural thresholds in other IP areas that may affect multi-claim strategies.
